The company can raise its initial capital from founding members, then gradually supplement it with retained earnings, new shareholders, documented shareholder loans, or appropriately structured external financing.

7. Vehicle acquisition and transport business plan

The first major investment should be a vehicle selected according to the work it can reliably generate, rather than personal preference.

7.1 Choosing the right vehicle

Option A: Sedan

Suitable for business travel, scheduled transportation and certain contracted passenger services.

Advantage: potentially lower operating costs. Limitation: lower passenger and cargo capacity.

Option B: Minivan

Suitable for group transport, staff transportation and some business delivery applications.

Advantage: broader commercial uses. Limitation: potentially higher acquisition and maintenance costs.

Option C: Light commercial vehicle

Suitable for deliveries, transporting equipment and supporting technical projects.

Advantage: supports both transport and engineering operations. Limitation: depends on suitable cargo contracts and local demand.

Before purchasing, obtain at least three written quotations and compare the total cost of ownership, not just the purchase price.

Evaluate:

  • Purchase price, vehicle age, condition, and inspection results.

  • Fuel consumption and likely monthly mileage.

  • Insurance, registration, taxes, maintenance, and replacement parts.

  • Driver availability, salary, licensing, and operating permissions.

  • Customer demand, contract duration, and payment reliability.

  • Expected downtime, resale value, and financing costs.

  • Whether a company vehicle can legally be used for the intended passenger or cargo service.

7.2 Operating strategy

The preferred model is a pre-contracted vehicle service, rather than purchasing a vehicle and hoping that customers will appear.

The proposed sequence is:

  1. Interview prospective business customers and identify specific transport needs.

  2. Obtain expressions of interest or written contract proposals.

  3. Calculate monthly operating costs for each vehicle option.

  4. Determine the minimum monthly revenue required to break even.

  5. Purchase only after the shareholders approve the business case.

  6. Track mileage, fuel, trips, repairs, receipts and customer payments.

  7. Review profitability every month.

A vehicle should be treated as a productive company asset, not as a personal benefit for any founding member.

Calculate your vehicle's break-even point

The company should know the minimum monthly sales required to cover the vehicle's operating expenses.

If monthly fixed costs are ETB 25,000, the vehicle generates ETB 600 in contribution per billable day after variable costs, and the target is to cover fixed costs, then:

Break-even billable days=25,000600≈41.7\text{Break-even billable days} = \frac{25,000}{600} \approx 41.7Break-even billable days=60025,000​≈41.7

This example would require approximately 42 billable days, which is not feasible in a normal month for a single vehicle. That indicates that either the contract rate must increase, the variable costs must decrease, or the fixed costs must be restructured.

The lesson is to calculate profitability using realistic billable days and contract pricing before committing capital.

9.4 Cash-flow and profit distribution policy

The company should not distribute all revenue or all accounting profit to shareholders.

The recommended order for allocating cash is:

  1. Pay operating expenses, salaries, taxes, insurance and outstanding liabilities.

  2. Maintain an adequate reserve for repairs, vehicle replacement, and unexpected costs.

  3. Reinvest in profitable technical services and necessary equipment.

  4. Make any approved loan repayments.

  5. Distribute dividends only from legally distributable profits after the required approvals and provisions.

Dividends should be based on the shareholders' rights and the company's approved accounts, not on how much cash happens to be in the bank.

9.5 Capital growth strategy

A sensible growth sequence is to build one profitable service at a time:

  • Use the vehicle to establish reliable cash flow.

  • Use existing member expertise to win IT and software projects with relatively low startup costs.

  • Build a portfolio of recurring customers.

  • Accumulate a reserve for technical tools, qualified staff and working capital.

  • Acquire another vehicle only when demand and projected returns justify it.

  • Enter larger engineering projects only after the company has sufficient capital, expertise and relevant approvals.

14. Governance and transparency policy

Since the company depends on contributions from multiple people, financial trust will be as important as commercial success.

Adopt these rules from the beginning:

  1. No personal use of company funds. Every withdrawal must have a legitimate business purpose and supporting documentation.

  2. Dual authorization. Significant transfers and purchases should require approval by two authorized people.

  3. Monthly reporting. Shareholders should receive a financial summary showing revenue, expenses, cash balances, liabilities and major assets.

  4. Asset register. Record the purchase price, registration documents, insurance, maintenance history and ownership of every major asset.

  5. Independent review. Arrange an independent accountant or auditor as required by law and appropriate to the company's size.

  6. Written contracts. Document employment, customer engagements, subcontracting and shareholder loans.

  7. Conflicts of interest. Require directors and managers to disclose personal interests in suppliers, contractors or customers.

  8. No guaranteed returns. Make clear that contributions to equity involve business risk and that dividends depend on actual performance and applicable law.

For members living abroad, use secure electronic reporting and hold regular online meetings so that distance does not reduce transparency or participation.

15. Long-term growth strategy

The company should gradually evolve from an asset-based business into a multidisciplinary engineering and technology provider.

Growth pillar 1: Software products

Develop reusable business software for inventory, transport management, customer relationship management, accounting workflows, and other validated Ethiopian business needs. Generate recurring revenue through maintenance and licensing where commercially appropriate.

Growth pillar 2: Energy solutions

Establish partnerships with qualified electrical contractors and energy providers. Start with suitable maintenance and installation projects before considering larger renewable energy investments.

Growth pillar 3: Telecom and IT infrastructure

Build a track record in enterprise networking, server systems, cybersecurity, backup and recovery, and eligible telecommunications subcontracting.

Growth pillar 4: Asset expansion

Expand the transport fleet only when utilization, cash flow and customer contracts support the purchase. Consider leasing or subcontracting where this provides better returns than owning every asset.

A separate department should have its own budget and performance targets. If a service line consistently loses money, management should correct it or suspend it rather than allowing it to consume capital from profitable activities.

16. Final recommendation to the founding members

The proposed company has the potential to become more than a vehicle investment group. It can become a long-term platform through which Ethiopian professionals combine capital, technical knowledge, and professional relationships to create sustainable businesses.

However, success will depend on three decisions made before the first major investment:

  • Choose a realistic starting business. Confirm that the vehicle can generate sufficient revenue to cover all operating and ownership costs.

  • Protect the relationship among members. Put ownership, decision-making, contributions, withdrawals and dividends in writing.

  • Build technical revenue early. Use the members' engineering and IT skills to win service contracts while the vehicle business establishes cash flow.

My preferred approach is to launch the company with one vehicle, a lean management structure, a strict financial-control system, and two initial business lines: contracted transport and IT/software services. Electrical, energy, and telecommunications services should expand as qualified personnel, capital and customer demand become available.

The first year should be judged by whether the company can operate reliably, maintain transparent accounts, pay its expenses, retain customers, and establish a profitable technical service line—not merely by whether it purchases a vehicle.

Since members will contribute different amounts, ownership should be calculated from the equity that each member actually commits under the approved share terms.

Use this formula:

These percentages assume the entire ETB 9 million consists of equity, with all contributions receiving the same economic rights per birr invested.

For example, a member investing ETB 500,000 into a company with ETB 9 million in total equity would own approximately 5.56%, assuming no different share classes, dilution, or other agreed adjustments.

4.3 Distinguish equity from shareholder loans

Not every member contribution needs to be treated as equity, but the decision must be made before money is collected.

  • Equity: represents ownership and potential dividend rights.

  • Shareholder loan: represents money lent to the company under agreed repayment and interest terms.

  • Future capital commitment: a promise to contribute later; it is not current cash.

A member who contributes more should not automatically receive interest-free repayment rights, additional voting rights, or a guaranteed return unless those terms are explicitly and legally agreed.

For a first-time company, I recommend keeping the initial structure simple: equity contributions for the core capital, with shareholder loans used only where a documented reason exists and the members approve the terms.

4.4 Shareholder agreement

Before registering the company or accepting substantial contributions, the founders should agree on:

  1. Ownership percentage and the rights attached to each share.

  2. Contribution deadlines and treatment of unpaid commitments.

  3. Voting rights, board appointments, and major decisions.

  4. Dividend policy and the reinvestment of profits.

  5. Share transfers, member exits, death, incapacity, and disputes.

  6. Related-party transactions and conflicts of interest.

  7. The treatment of shareholder loans and any future capital calls.

  8. Company asset ownership, intellectual property, and confidentiality.

  9. The procedures for admitting new members and managing dilution.

  10. Dispute resolution and company dissolution.

The memorandum and articles of association should be consistent with the shareholder agreement. They should not rely on informal WhatsApp messages or verbal understandings to establish ownership.

4.5 Special consideration for members abroad

Being an Ethiopian citizen living abroad does not, by itself, establish every applicable investment classification or exemption.

Ethiopia's Investment Proclamation No. 1180/2020 includes an Ethiopian permanently residing abroad who elects foreign-investor treatment within its definition of a foreign investor. Investment-permit and capital requirements may therefore depend on the member's chosen status, the business activity, and the way the investment is structured.

The company should maintain a rolling 13-week cash-flow forecast that records:

  • Planned equipment purchases and debt repayments.

Years 3–4 — Expand engineering capability

An illustrative planning scenario anticipates annual revenue of ETB 2.60 million in Year 1, ETB 4.00 million in Year 2 and ETB 5.80 million in Year 3. Corresponding operating surpluses are estimated at ETB 0.30 million, ETB 0.75 million and ETB 1.25 million.

These figures are not guaranteed outcomes and must be revised using actual quotations, customer contracts and operating results.

Dividends may be distributed only from legally distributable profits following the required approvals and after providing for liabilities and necessary reserves. Revenue and bank balances will not automatically be treated as distributable profits.

9. Risk Management

The company recognizes the following principal risks:

  • Insufficient customer demand.

  • Vehicle breakdown and unexpected maintenance costs.

  • Inflation and changes in operating expenses.

  • Delayed customer payments.

  • Disagreements among shareholders.

  • Insufficient working capital.

  • Inadequate technical qualifications or regulatory permissions.

  • Poor financial controls and misuse of company assets.

The company will mitigate these risks through written shareholder agreements, customer contracts, independent vehicle inspections, adequate reserves, monthly financial reporting, dual payment authorization and compliance with applicable laws.

10. Legal and Regulatory Compliance

Before commencing commercial activities, the founders will confirm the appropriate company structure and complete the required registration, TIN, trade licensing and tax procedures.

The company will verify the permits and competency requirements applicable to transport, telecommunications, electrical engineering and other regulated activities.

Members living abroad will provide the necessary documentation, and the company will confirm any additional investment classification or foreign-investment requirements that may apply to individual members.

The company will maintain proper accounting, employment, tax and statutory records and renew its licenses as required.

11. Twelve-Month Implementation Plan

Months 1–2: Founders' agreement and market validation

Confirm ownership, share value, contribution commitments, management responsibilities and the proposed business name. Interview prospective customers and obtain vehicle quotations.

Month 3: Registration and capital collection

Complete the required company formation procedures, establish the company bank account and record shareholder contributions.

Month 4: Procurement decision

Select the vehicle only after the approved financial assessment, customer demand review and independent inspection.

Months 5–6: Launch

Begin authorized transport operations and deliver initial IT support or software projects.

Months 7–9: Customer development

Pursue recurring maintenance contracts, improve transport utilization and develop partnerships with qualified technical service providers.

Months 10–12: Financial review and expansion planning

Prepare annual accounts, evaluate business performance, review the shareholder register and approve the second-year operating plan.

The schedule is a planning target and may change according to registration, funding and procurement requirements.

12. Performance Measurement

Management will report monthly on:

  • Capital received and shareholder records.

  • Transport utilization and operating profitability.

  • Technical service revenue and recurring contracts.

  • Customer acquisition and payment collection.

  • Cash-flow position and working capital.

  • Operating expenses and asset maintenance.

  • Compliance status and outstanding obligations.

  • Progress against the approved business plan.

The board or governing body will review performance quarterly and recommend corrective actions when results fall below the approved plan.

13. Long-Term Development

The company will grow in stages.

During Year 1, the priority will be establishing reliable transport operations, winning technical projects and maintaining financial discipline.

During Years 2–3, the company will aim to expand recurring IT support, software development, networking and qualified engineering subcontracting.

During Years 3–5, the company may consider additional vehicles, larger technical projects, renewable energy services and proprietary software products where customer demand, capital availability and regulatory requirements support expansion.

14. Conclusion

EthioTech Engineering & Solutions PLC is proposed as a collaborative investment platform through which Ethiopian professionals can combine financial resources, technical expertise and business relationships.

The company's initial success will depend on transparent ownership, disciplined capital allocation, reliable customer service and careful management of the relationship between transport operations and technical services.

The founding members commit to reviewing and approving the final share structure, confirming the initial budget, completing the necessary legal procedures and establishing appropriate financial controls before commencing commercial operations.

Approval by the founding members

Before the founders sign this proposal, the three most important items to confirm are the actual monetary value of one share, whether the proposed ETB 4.25 million capital will be fully paid, and whether the vehicle purchase can be supported without compromising working capital.

1. Project overview

1.1 Purpose

Develop a secure, interactive web application that supports two related business needs:

  1. Public-facing website: Introduce the company, advertise its services, display its projects and capabilities, and generate customer inquiries.

  2. Private management portal: Allow authorized shareholders and employees to manage capital, ownership records, vehicles, jobs, projects, expenses, invoices, documents, and reports.

The application should support the company's initial operations and expand as it enters new business areas.

1.2 Business objectives

  • Establish a professional digital presence for the company.

  • Maintain accurate shareholder and capital-contribution records.

  • Track the acquisition, utilization, maintenance, and operating costs of company vehicles.

  • Manage IT support, networking, software development, electrical, and engineering projects.

  • Record revenue, expenses, invoices, payments, and outstanding balances.

  • Improve transparency and accountability among founding members.

  • Give management timely information for business decisions.

  • Provide a foundation for future mobile, accounting, and customer-service integrations.

Architecture recommendation: Since the company will handle ownership and financial records, use React for the user interface and Django REST Framework for the backend. Do not store business records only in browser storage or rely on frontend checks for security.

2. Product scope and user types

The platform should use a single application with public pages and an authenticated management portal.

2.1 Public website

The public website should be accessible without login and include:

  • Technology and engineering capabilities

  • Contact page and inquiry form

  • Careers or partnership page, if required

  • Privacy policy and terms of use

  • Shareholder login link

Do not publicly display private shareholder phone numbers, personal documents, internal financial reports, or non-public company records.

2.2 Private portal

The management portal should support the following user groups.

Role

Main responsibilities

System administrator

Shareholder

View permitted ownership, capital, reports, meeting records and notices

General manager

Transport manager

Sales and customer-service officer

Leads, customer records, quotations and service requests

Auditor or read-only reviewer

Access approved reports and audit records without editing business data

Access must be configurable. A user can have more than one role if the company authorizes it. For example, the general manager might also be a shareholder, but their permissions should remain distinct.

3. Functional requirements

Each feature below should be treated as a requirement to implement and test.

3.1 Authentication and user management

Requirements

  • Users can sign in and sign out securely.

  • Administrators can invite users and deactivate accounts.

  • Users can request password resets.

  • The application can enforce strong password policies.

  • Sessions expire according to the security configuration.

  • Sensitive actions require permission checks on the backend.

  • The system records login events and security-related changes.

  • Account status supports active, inactive, suspended, and invited states.

  • The interface displays only the pages and actions the current user is permitted to use.

Acceptance criteria

  • An unauthenticated user cannot open protected pages or retrieve protected API data.

  • A shareholder cannot edit financial records unless explicitly authorized.

  • Deactivating a user prevents further access without deleting the historical business records associated with that user.

  • Password-reset tokens expire and cannot be reused.

3.2 Shareholder and ownership management

Create a shareholder register with the following fields:

  • Shareholder ID

  • Full legal name

  • Email and phone, stored privately

  • Country of residence, where needed

  • Number of shares

  • Share price and currency

  • Agreed capital commitment

  • Amount paid

  • Outstanding contribution

  • Ownership percentage

  • Admission date

  • Shareholder status

  • Signed agreements and related documents

Ownership percentage should be calculated from the total issued shares:

Ownership percentage = shareholder shares / total issued shares × 100

If the founders approve a price of ETB 250,000 per share, the implied total capital is ETB 4,250,000. Treat this amount as a planning assumption until it is formally approved and legally documented.

Required functions

  • Add, edit, view, and deactivate shareholder records.

  • Record capital commitments and actual payments separately.

  • Attach receipts and signed agreements.

  • Show paid, partially paid, and unpaid contribution balances.

  • Generate a shareholder statement.

  • Produce a printable shareholder register.

  • Maintain historical ownership changes rather than overwriting them.

  • Restrict changes to shares, share transfers, and capital commitments to authorized users.

  • Require approval and supporting documentation for ownership changes.

Important business rule: The system must distinguish issued shares, authorized shares, promised contributions, paid-in capital, and outstanding contributions. These are not interchangeable.

3.3 Capital contribution management

Each contribution record should contain:

  • Unique transaction number

  • Shareholder

  • Amount

  • Currency

  • Contribution date

  • Payment method

  • Reference or receipt number

  • Supporting attachment

  • Recorded by

  • Approval status

  • Approval history

Workflow

  1. Finance officer records a contribution.

  2. Supporting evidence is attached.

  3. An authorized reviewer verifies the transaction.

  4. Once approved, the payment appears in contribution summaries.

  5. Corrections use an adjustment or reversal record with an explanation; approved transactions should not be silently deleted.

The dashboard should show:

  • Total agreed capital

  • Total capital received

  • Outstanding capital

  • Percentage collected

  • Contributions by shareholder

  • Recent contribution transactions

Do not automatically classify all incoming money as share capital. Loans from members, reimbursable advances, and other funding arrangements should have separate transaction types.

3.4 Transport and fleet management

The company plans to start with transport services. This module should track the vehicle as a business asset and manage the operational details of each trip.

Vehicle records

  • Vehicle ID and registration number

  • Make, model, year, and category

  • Purchase price and purchase date

  • Odometer reading

  • Ownership or lease status

  • Insurance details and expiry date

  • Registration and inspection dates

  • Assigned driver

  • Current status: available, booked, on trip, maintenance, inactive

  • Acquisition documents and photographs

Trip records

  • Trip number

  • Customer

  • Pickup and destination

  • Start and end dates

  • Driver and assigned vehicle

  • Contracted price

  • Fuel and other trip expenses

  • Odometer at departure and return

Maintenance records

  • Vehicle

  • Service date and odometer

  • Parts and labor costs

  • Next service date or odometer

  • Invoice or receipt

  • Approval status

Transport reports

  • Trips completed by period

  • Revenue by vehicle

  • Fuel and maintenance expenses

  • Vehicle utilization

  • Outstanding customer invoices

  • Upcoming insurance, registration, and maintenance dates

  • Profitability by trip or contract

Business rules

  • Prevent overlapping bookings for the same vehicle where dates and availability conflict.

  • Warn users about expired or soon-to-expire documents.

  • Keep the full history of vehicle expenses and maintenance.

  • Do not mark a trip complete until the required trip information is supplied.

  • Allow a manager to override a booking conflict only with a recorded reason and appropriate permission.

Because the company has multiple founding members, provide a dedicated governance module.

Voting, quorum, approval thresholds, and shareholder rights must be configurable according to the company's legally adopted governing documents. Do not assume that every decision uses one vote per share or that all matters are decided by a simple majority.

The platform should provide filterable reports for:

Users should be able to filter by date range, division, status, customer, vehicle, or project where relevant.

Reports should show the generation date, applied filters, currency, and any important accounting limitations. Only authorized users may export sensitive information.

5. UI/UX and visual design specification

The interface should feel modern, professional, fast, and suitable for both office computers and mobile devices.

5.1 Design direction

  • Use a clean light theme as the default.

  • Use a dark navy or charcoal sidebar and restrained blue or teal accents.

  • Use neutral page backgrounds, readable typography, and consistent spacing.

  • Use clear status badges and accessible color contrast.

  • Keep charts simple and label them clearly.

  • Avoid excessive animation, oversized cards, and decorative effects that make financial work harder.

  • Offer a dark theme as a later enhancement if it does not delay essential functionality.

5.2 Core UI components

Build reusable components rather than implementing every screen independently:

  • AppShell

  • Sidebar

  • Topbar

  • Breadcrumbs

  • PageHeader

  • DataTable

  • FilterBar

  • SearchInput

  • DateRangeFilter

  • StatusBadge

  • FormDrawer or FormDialog

All interactive controls must work. Buttons that are not yet implemented should not appear as if they are functional.

5.3 Dashboard design

The dashboard should change according to the user's role.

For management, display:

  • Total capital committed and received

  • Revenue and expenses for the selected period

  • Outstanding customer balances

  • Active projects and overdue tasks

  • Transport trips and vehicle availability

  • Pending approvals

  • Recent activities

  • Revenue trend chart

  • Performance by business division

For shareholders, show only the information approved for shareholder access, such as ownership, their contribution status, company announcements, and approved reports.

For technical staff, prioritize assigned tasks, deadlines, active projects, and recent comments.

For the finance officer, prioritize pending transactions, invoices, contribution records, reconciliation tasks, and financial summaries.

5.4 Responsive requirements

  • Desktop: full sidebar and multi-column dashboard.

  • Tablet: collapsible sidebar and adapted card layout.

  • Mobile: compact navigation, stacked cards, usable forms, and horizontally scrollable or responsive data tables.

  • Forms should have clear labels and validation messages.

  • Important actions must be accessible by keyboard.

  • Never use color as the only indicator of a record's status.

5.5 Interaction behavior

  • Confirm before destructive or financially consequential actions.

  • Show clear success and failure messages.

  • Preserve form input when a recoverable submission fails.

  • Provide loading, empty, error, and success states.

  • Use pagination for large datasets.

  • Debounce search inputs where appropriate.

  • Ask for confirmation when leaving a form with unsaved changes.

  • Require a reason for approved-record reversals or administrative overrides.

6. Technical architecture

Use a three-layer architecture: React frontend, Django REST API, and PostgreSQL database.

Frontend — React + TypeScript

Pages · Forms · Tables · Charts · Client-side validation

Backend — Django REST Framework

Authentication · Permissions · Business rules · API · Audit logging

Data and file storage

PostgreSQL · Private document storage · Backups

6.1 Frontend responsibilities

React should handle:

  • Page rendering and navigation

  • Form input and client-side validation

  • Tables, filtering, pagination, and sorting

  • Charts and visual summaries

  • Loading and error states

  • Role-aware presentation

  • Responsive layout and accessibility

React must not be the final authority for access control, financial calculations, ownership changes, or transaction approval.

6.2 Backend responsibilities

Django REST Framework should handle:

  • Authentication and session management

  • User roles and object-level permissions

  • Database operations and validation

  • Business rules and transaction integrity

  • Capital and ownership calculations

  • Approval workflows

  • File access authorization

  • Audit logs

  • Report generation

  • API rate limits and security protections

6.3 Database responsibilities

PostgreSQL should store structured records with foreign keys, constraints, indexes, and transactions. Financial changes and ownership updates should be performed atomically where required.

Use database migrations to track schema changes. Never modify production database tables manually without a controlled migration and backup.

7.1 Database design rules

  1. Use a unique internal ID for every business record.

  2. Use foreign keys to enforce relationships.

  3. Store money as a fixed-precision decimal, not a floating-point number.

  4. Store timestamps consistently, preferably in UTC, and display them in the configured local timezone.

  5. Store dates separately when they represent a business date rather than a precise instant.

  6. Store currency explicitly on monetary records.

  7. Use controlled status values instead of free-form text wherever possible.

  8. Keep approved financial transactions and ownership events historically traceable.

  9. Use soft deactivation for records that must remain in historical reports.

  10. Index frequently filtered fields, such as transaction date, status, customer, project, and vehicle.

  11. Store files outside ordinary database rows, keeping metadata and protected storage keys in the database.

  12. Use explicit versioning or event records for changes that must be reconstructed later.

7.2 Ownership calculation

Do not simply add up every historical share issuance and transfer without accounting for cancellations and transfers. The authoritative ownership calculation must reflect the currently valid share register.

For the initial scenario:

  • Total proposed shares: 17

  • One-share allocation: approximately 5.88%

  • Two-share allocation: approximately 11.76%

The database should distinguish proposed allocations from legally issued shares. The application should not mark shares as officially issued until the required company approvals and records have been completed.

8. API design

Use a versioned REST API with a consistent JSON response format. A base path such as /api/v1/ allows future versions to evolve without breaking existing clients.

GET /api/v1/customers/, POST /api/v1/customers/

Leads

GET /api/v1/leads/, POST /api/v1/leads/, PATCH /api/v1/leads/{id}/

Vehicles

GET /api/v1/vehicles/, POST /api/v1/vehicles/, PATCH /api/v1/vehicles/{id}/

Trips

GET /api/v1/trips/, POST /api/v1/trips/, POST /api/v1/trips/{id}/complete/

Projects

GET /api/v1/projects/, POST /api/v1/projects/, PATCH /api/v1/projects/{id}/

Tasks

GET /api/v1/tasks/, POST /api/v1/tasks/, PATCH /api/v1/tasks/{id}/

Expenses

GET /api/v1/expenses/, POST /api/v1/expenses/, POST /api/v1/expenses/{id}/approve/

Invoices

GET /api/v1/invoices/, POST /api/v1/invoices/, GET /api/v1/invoices/{id}/

Documents

GET /api/v1/documents/, POST /api/v1/documents/, GET /api/v1/documents/{id}/download/

Reports

GET /api/v1/reports/overview/, GET /api/v1/reports/finance/, GET /api/v1/reports/fleet/

Audit

GET /api/v1/audit-logs/

Notifications

GET /api/v1/notifications/, POST /api/v1/notifications/{id}/read/

These are proposed endpoint names, not pre-existing services. Implement them with explicit serializers, permissions, validation, and tests.

8.2 API conventions

  • Use appropriate HTTP methods: GET, POST, PATCH, and DELETE only when deletion is allowed.

  • Use consistent error responses and meaningful HTTP status codes.

  • Validate all submitted data on the server.

  • Support pagination, filtering, and sorting on list endpoints.

  • Avoid returning unnecessary personal or financial fields.

  • Document the API with OpenAPI/Swagger tooling.

  • Use transactions for multi-step financial and ownership operations.

  • Make approval and reversal actions explicit endpoints rather than generic record updates.

  • Apply idempotency protection to payment ingestion or other operations where retries could duplicate a transaction.

8.3 Example response

A shareholder list response could follow this structure:

JSON
{
  "count": 14,
  "results": [
    {
      "id": "sh_001",
      "full_name": "Example Shareholder",
      "shares": 2,
      "ownership_percentage": "11.7647",
      "committed_capital": "500000.00",
      "paid_capital": "250000.00",
      "currency": "ETB",
      "status": "active"
    }
  ]
}

This is illustrative data. Production responses must use actual database records and must not expose records to unauthorized users.

9. React project structure

A modular structure will make the frontend easier to maintain as the company expands.

Plain text
ethio-tech-platform/ ├── frontend/ │ ├── public/ │ ├── src/ │ │ ├── app/ │ │ │ ├── router.tsx │ │ │ ├── providers.tsx │ │ │ └── query-client.ts │ │ ├── components/ │ │ │ ├── ui/ │ │ │ ├── layout/ │ │ │ ├── forms/ │ │ │ ├── tables/ │ │ │ └── feedback/ │ │ ├── features/ │ │ │ ├── auth/ │ │ │ ├── dashboard/ │ │ │ ├── shareholders/ │ │ │ ├── contributions/ │ │ │ ├── customers/ │ │ │ ├── fleet/ │ │ │ ├── projects/ │ │ │ ├── finance/ │ │ │ ├── documents/ │ │ │ ├── meetings/ │ │ │ ├── reports/ │ │ │ └── settings/ │ │ ├── hooks/ │ │ ├── lib/ │ │ │ ├── api-client.ts │ │ │ ├── formatters.ts │ │ │ └── permissions.ts │ │ ├── types/ │ │ ├── styles/ │ │ └── main.tsx │ ├── package.json │ └── vite.config.ts ├── backend/ │ ├── config/ │ ├── apps/ │ │ ├── accounts/ │ │ ├── shareholders/ │ │ ├── contributions/ │ │ ├── customers/ │ │ ├── fleet/ │ │ ├── projects/ │ │ ├── finance/ │ │ ├── documents/ │ │ ├── governance/ │ │ ├── notifications/ │ │ └── audit/ │ ├── manage.py │ └── requirements.txt ├── infrastructure/ │ ├── docker/ │ └── deployment/ ├── docs/ │ ├── requirements.md │ ├── api.md │ ├── database.md │ └── user-guide.md ├── .env.example ├── .gitignore └── README.md

Organize features around business domains. Avoid placing every component, API function, and type in a single large file.

10. Frontend implementation standards

10.1 Data fetching

Use TanStack Query for server data, caching, retries where appropriate, and invalidating affected records after successful mutations.

For example, after approving a contribution:

  1. Submit the approval request to the API.

  2. Show a loading state.

  3. Display the result returned by the server.

  4. Invalidate the relevant contribution and dashboard queries.

  5. Refresh the displayed totals from the server.

  6. Show a useful error message if approval fails.

Do not update financial totals permanently using client-only calculations.

10.2 Form validation

Use React Hook Form and Zod to provide fast client-side feedback. Repeat all important validation on the backend.

Examples of validation rules:

  • A monetary amount must be greater than zero unless the transaction type explicitly permits a zero amount.

  • An invoice due date must follow the applicable issue-date rules.

  • A trip must reference a valid vehicle and authorized driver.

  • A task deadline should be checked against relevant project dates.

  • A shareholder allocation must pass the approved share-register rules.

  • An uploaded file must satisfy file-size, content-type, and access-policy restrictions.

10.3 State management

Use local React state for UI interactions such as open dialogs and selected tabs. Use server-state tools for data retrieved from the backend. Introduce a global client-state library only if the application demonstrates a real need for it.

Never use localStorage as the source of truth for shareholder records, payments, permissions, or other authoritative business data.

10.4 Reusable formatting

Create centralized utilities for:

  • ETB currency formatting

  • Date and time formatting

  • Percentage formatting

  • Number formatting

  • Status labels

  • API error messages

The system should display ETB for Ethiopian birr transactions, while allowing other currencies where legitimately needed. Do not silently convert currencies without an explicitly selected exchange rate, source, and date.

11. Security, privacy, and reliability

Security must be designed into the application rather than added at the end.

11.1 Authentication and authorization

  • Prefer secure, HTTP-only, secure, appropriately configured SameSite cookies when using session-based authentication.

  • Protect state-changing session requests against CSRF.

  • If token authentication is selected, define token storage, expiration, rotation, and revocation carefully.

  • Enforce authorization on every protected backend endpoint.

  • Check both role permissions and access to the specific object.

  • Apply least-privilege access by default.

  • Use multi-factor authentication for privileged users where practical.

  • Rate-limit login, password-reset, and sensitive endpoints.

11.2 Data protection

  • Enforce HTTPS in production.

  • Keep credentials and secret keys outside source control.

  • Use separate development, testing, and production configurations.

  • Restrict database access to authorized application services.

  • Encrypt sensitive backups and storage where feasible.

  • Store documents in private storage and issue authorized downloads.

  • Avoid putting passwords, access tokens, full personal details, or unnecessary financial information in logs.

  • Establish retention and deletion policies consistent with legal and business requirements.

11.3 Financial and governance integrity

  • Require appropriate approval for financial transactions.

  • Keep immutable or tamper-evident audit history for important events.

  • Record who performed each sensitive action and when.

  • Use database transactions to prevent partial updates.

  • Reconcile transaction records against bank and payment evidence.

  • Prevent the requester from approving their own high-risk transaction where segregation of duties is required.

  • Require a documented correction process for approved transactions.

11.4 Backup and recovery

Define and test a backup policy before production launch.

At minimum:

  • Automated database backups

  • Protected document backups

  • Encrypted backup storage

  • Restricted access to backup files

  • Periodic restoration tests

  • A documented recovery procedure

  • Agreed recovery-point and recovery-time objectives

A backup is not proven useful until a restoration test succeeds.

11.5 Performance and availability

The application should:

  • Paginate large datasets.

  • Avoid unnecessary API requests and repeated database queries.

  • Compress and appropriately size images.

  • Use indexes for frequently queried data.

  • Show useful errors when the server is unavailable.

  • Record application errors and operational health metrics.

  • Support migration and deployment procedures that minimize avoidable downtime.

Set measurable performance targets during development, then validate them with representative data and real user workflows.

12. Testing strategy

Testing should cover the frontend, backend, database behavior, permissions, and complete workflows.

Test level

Recommended tools

Examples

Vitest, pytest

Component tests

React Testing Library

Integration tests

12.1 Minimum acceptance scenarios

The application is not ready for release until the following work correctly:

  1. A user can log in and see the correct role-specific dashboard.

  2. A shareholder can see only authorized ownership and contribution information.

  3. Finance can record and approve contributions with an auditable history.

  4. An unauthorized user cannot approve their own restricted financial transaction.

  5. A manager can register a vehicle and record maintenance.

  6. The system warns about vehicle document expiry.

  7. A customer inquiry submitted on the public website appears in the private CRM.

  8. An authorized user can create a project and assign tasks.

  9. An invoice can be recorded and its outstanding balance calculated correctly.

  10. A protected document cannot be downloaded by an unauthorized user.

  11. Financial and ownership corrections retain the relevant audit trail.

  12. Reports respect filters, permissions, and selected date ranges.

  13. The core workflows function on desktop and mobile screens.

  14. Backup restoration has been tested successfully.

13. Development roadmap

Build the application incrementally. Do not attempt to implement every module simultaneously.

Phase 1 — Foundation

Weeks 1–2 · Planning and architecture

  • Finalize requirements and user roles.

  • Create the React/Vite frontend and Django backend.

  • Configure PostgreSQL and migrations.

  • Establish the design system, routing, authentication, and permissions.

Phase 2 — Company administration

Weeks 3–4 · Ownership and governance

  • Shareholder register

  • Capital contributions

  • User management

  • Documents, meetings, and audit logging

Phase 3 — Business operations

Weeks 5–7 · Transport and projects

  • Vehicles, drivers, trips, and maintenance

  • Customers and sales inquiries

  • Projects, tasks, and technical deliverables

Phase 4 — Finance and reporting

Weeks 8–9 · Financial controls

  • Expenses, invoices, and payments

  • Approval workflows

  • Management dashboard and reports

Phase 5 — Release and stabilization

Weeks 10–12 · Testing and deployment

  • End-to-end and security testing

  • Data migration and user training

  • Production deployment and backup verification

  • Fix defects and prepare the user guide

These estimates assume a reasonably experienced developer or small team and a controlled first release. Actual duration will depend on developer experience, design complexity, integrations, and the completeness of the business requirements.

14. Deployment and DevOps

14.1 Environments

Maintain separate environments for:

  • Development: Local coding and experimentation.

  • Testing/staging: User acceptance testing with non-production data.

  • Production: Real company operations and records.

Never use real shareholder financial data in a public demo or unprotected testing environment.

14.2 Deployment requirements

  • Build the React frontend for production.

  • Run Django through a production-grade application server.

  • Use Nginx or an equivalent reverse proxy where appropriate.

  • Run PostgreSQL in a protected environment.

  • Configure HTTPS and domain settings.

  • Store secrets in environment variables or a secrets manager.

  • Apply database migrations through a controlled deployment process.

  • Configure backups, logging, monitoring, and error reporting.

  • Keep a documented rollback plan for failed releases.

14.3 Suggested repository workflow

Use Git branches and pull requests:

  • main — production-ready code

  • develop — integration branch, if needed

  • feature/shareholder-management

  • feature/fleet-management

  • feature/project-management

  • feature/finance-module

  • fix/... — bug fixes

Require code review for sensitive changes involving authentication, permissions, financial records, ownership calculations, or deployment configuration.

15. Business rules and decisions to finalize

Before implementing the relevant modules, the founders should approve the following decisions.

Decision

Why it matters

Final legal company name and entity type

Determines official records and legal terminology

Approved share classes and share value

Determines the ownership and capital model

Share issuance and transfer rules

Determines how ownership changes are represented

Approval thresholds

Determines who can authorize expenses and other decisions

Financial reporting basis

Determines how management reports should be calculated

Vehicle ownership or leasing model

Determines acquisition and operating workflows

Service divisions

Determines project categories, budgets, and reporting

User access policies

Protects shareholder and customer information

Document retention

Determines how long records must be retained

Currency and tax configuration

Prevents incorrect financial calculations

Company timezone and reporting calendar

Ensures consistent dates and period reports

Backup and recovery targets

Determines infrastructure and operating costs

For an Ethiopian company, the legal form, shareholder rights, accounting treatment, tax configuration, licensing obligations, and applicable privacy requirements should be reviewed with qualified local professionals before the application is used for official records.

16. Future enhancements

Once the core system is stable, consider these additions.

  • Customer portal: Customers can request services, review quotations, and track approved work.

  • Driver interface: Drivers can view assigned trips, submit expenses, and upload delivery confirmations.

  • GPS integration: Track vehicle locations through a suitable authorized provider.

  • Mobile application: Use React Native or another appropriate mobile framework if a dedicated app becomes necessary.

  • Accounting integration: Synchronize approved transactions with a compatible accounting system.

  • Procurement and inventory: Track technical equipment, spare parts, purchases, and suppliers.

  • Power and engineering operations: Add asset maintenance schedules, inspection workflows, and project-specific reporting.

  • Advanced analytics: Analyze service profitability, vehicle utilization, customer retention, and project delivery.

  • Multilingual support: Add English and Amharic interfaces if required.

  • AI-assisted operations: Introduce carefully controlled document extraction, inquiry classification, and report summaries after the core data model is reliable.

Do not start with AI, GPS, payroll, or complex integrations unless a real business need justifies the extra development and maintenance costs.

17. Recommended first-release screen list

Use this as the development checklist for the initial version.

Implementation checklist

Public website

Shared portal

Company administration

Business operations

Finance and reports

18. Definition of done

The initial version should be considered complete only when:

  • All agreed first-release screens are implemented.

  • The application works on desktop, tablet, and mobile.

  • Core workflows are connected to the backend and database.

  • Authentication and backend permissions have been tested.

  • Ownership and financial calculations pass tests with known expected results.

  • Sensitive documents cannot be accessed without authorization.

  • Critical actions produce audit records.

  • The application has loading, empty, error, and success states.

  • Business records can be searched, filtered, and reported accurately.

  • A tested backup and recovery process is available.

  • The deployment and configuration instructions are documented.

  • Administrators and end users have a basic user guide.

  • The company has approved the relevant policies and financial workflows.

19. Recommended development starting point

Start by building the application foundation, then implement one complete business workflow at a time. The first milestone should be authentication, the application shell, the dashboard, and the shareholder register.

A good first vertical slice is:

  1. Create the Django user model and permission setup.

  2. Create the shareholder database model and API.

  3. Build the React shareholder list and detail pages.

  4. Add create/edit forms with validation.

  5. Add pagination and search.

  6. Enforce backend permissions.

  7. Add tests for ownership calculations and unauthorized access.

  8. Add audit history for sensitive changes.

  9. Connect the dashboard to actual API data.

  10. Deploy the slice to a testing environment and validate it with representative users.

This approach establishes a reliable foundation before adding capital contributions, transport, projects, and finance.

Final recommendation: Treat the platform as a business system with financial and governance controls, not just a dashboard with attractive charts. Prioritize accurate records, permissions, traceability, and reliable workflows; build the visual experience around those foundations.
